title: Maybe it's not that serious
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez recalls a new manager telling her 'this isn't the operating room' after she had spent years in mission-driven workplaces that treated every email as an emergency. From that moment she built three working mottos: maybe it is not that serious, I am not that important, and sometimes the crisis is you. Her argument is that mission-driven leaders confuse the importance of the work with a need for constant panic, and that this burns people out without improving the work. The move that makes it leadership rather than self-help is the third motto, which asks leaders to examine honestly whether they are the gasoline on the fire. The piece ends on the claim that loosening the grip on seriousness and ego is how organisations become places people want to stay.
points: Mission-driven organisations tend to equate high stakes with permanent urgency, and that habit is cultural rather than necessary.
Caring about the work and treating each interaction as a crisis are separable, and leaders can keep the first while dropping the second.
Accepting that you are expendable relieves pressure and keeps ego from inflating small problems.
Leaders should ask daily whether they are contributing to a given crisis, which improved both her own well-being and that of those around her.
A calmer culture is a retention strategy: people stay where they can breathe and thrive.
quotes: Everyone took everything so seriously. This never quite felt right. But I kind of fell into it because, well, you just followed the status quo.
Well, the nice thing about our work? This isn’t the operating room. Sure, crises can happen from time to time, but that’s not the standard.
And sure—the work matters. But that doesn’t mean every freakin’ interaction needs to be ripe with panic and chaos.
Really, unless I’m in the operating room, or in some kind of other life-saving profession of sorts, I’m really not that important. Life at work will go on… with or without me (sorry, ego).
Ever looked around at all the fires and realized you were… dare I say it… the gasoline? Or maybe you weren’t doing all that, but you sure weren’t trying to find the fire extinguisher.
If we could just loosen our death grip on all of that, maybe we actually stand a chance at building workplaces people want to stay in. Offices where folks can breathe.
